fact: The Ministry of Health and Sanitation has rolled out the Malawi Health Care Information System (Mahis), a digital health records system meant to replace hard-copy health passport books, according to its director of quality management and digital health.
Mahis is in pilot phase at Queen Elizabeth Central Hospital in Blantyre and at selected health centres nationwide; the number of health centres is not given.

The newspaper's check at Queen Elizabeth Central Hospital's outpatient department found Mahis operational: registered patients no longer produced health passport books, and first-time patients had details captured at the registry and were issued a barcode; the ministry says each patient gets a unique identifier held on a server reachable by facilities through an interoperability layer.

Mahis was reported in pilot phase and live at Queen Elizabeth Central Hospital's outpatient department on 3 September 2026, with the ministry hoping most health facilities will be digitised within the next year or so.
Mahis is under pilot at selected health centres nationwide alongside one central hospital; no count or share of health centres is stated.

A project that began in December 2025 and runs to March 2027, with a kickoff event on 10 February 2026, will deploy DHIS2 climate and health tools (the Chap Modeling Platform and climate data integration) on the DHIS2-based national HMIS and the One Health surveillance platform, first in four districts, and link them to the WHO-supported EWARS; it is commissioned by BMZ and implemented by GIZ.

fact: A qualitative study in Zomba District (Taylor and Kazembe, BMC Health Services Research), with a focus group of 10 practitioners from 9 clinics in September 2024, found that most facilities, particularly rural government clinics, kept no out-patient files on their premises, so the paper, patient-held Health Passport, written by hand during consultation, was the only medical record for the majority of the population.

The Ministry of Health's framework calls MaHIS the ministry's flagship platform for managing health information and the cornerstone for harmonising fragmented EMR systems, and gives its Digital Health Division the job of overseeing its expansion, maintenance and user support.

The Digital Health Governance Framework 2025-2030, signed by the Secretary for Health in June 2025, names MaHIS and sets its nationwide scale-up across public and private facilities, integrated with the national ID system and hosted on e-Government data centres; it cites a Digital Health Policy 2024-2030 alongside.

The framework states that digital health in Malawi continues to rely heavily on donor funding, and sets a medium-term step of starting the transition from donor-funded to government-led systems; it says this of digital health systems generally, with no budget line given for MaHIS.
The framework describes central hospitals, the national referral tier, as key implementation sites for MaHIS, and says its rollout has been constrained; it gives no count of facilities at any tier.

UNDP's quarterly report describes the EMR systems as the Ministry of Health's, with the ministry's Digital Health Directorate leading the work to link them to the National Registration Bureau's unique identification numbers.

UNDP reports that on 30 June 2025 the Ministry of Health's senior management approved the lessons-learnt report on linking national ID and birth certificate numbers to electronic medical records, piloted in Karonga District, and recommended scaling the linkage to other districts nationwide.

BMZ reports that the openSRP electronic patient register was being piloted at one rural health centre, Bilira in Ntcheu District, with 23 tablets and about 10,000 patients covered, and that scaling to other facilities was still to be funded.

BMZ reports the openSRP e-register in use at a single rural health centre, Bilira, in its maternal, newborn and child health clinics, with an outpatient module in development; no other facility had it.

BMZ describes nurses at Bilira health centre opening or creating the patient's electronic record on a tablet during the consultation and following a step-by-step checklist that will not advance until the required value is entered.

fact: Countdown to 2030, with the Ministry of Health, gives no count or share of facilities entering their own reports; it puts completeness of monthly facility reporting in DHIS2 (mean of ANC, delivery and immunisation forms) at 97% of expected reports nationally in 2025, up from 83% in 2020, with 95% of districts at 90% or more, and an annual data-quality score of 87 against 73 in 2020.

The study states that since 2002 the Ministry of Health has collected and reported aggregated facility-level data through a unified HMIS under its Central Monitoring and Evaluation Division, which runs on DHIS2 and sets the reporting deadlines; no date is given for the present arrangement, so the document's published date is used.

The study states that as of January 2023, 1,266 health facilities, government-owned, private for-profit and private non-profit, were reporting in the HMIS on DHIS2 (an unpublished figure by its own citation), that some reports exist only at central hospitals, and that all 15 facilities of Neno district report, two hospitals and 13 health centres.

The study states that in practice paper reporting forms are distributed to health facilities, compiled there from programme registers, collected by data clerks and programme coordinators and entered into DHIS2 at the district HMIS office, although in theory any facility with electricity, internet and a computer could report online; no date is given, so the document's published date is used.

The study states that in November 2022 Neno district began decentralising DHIS2 data entry to its health centres in a step-wedge process; it gives no count of the district's 13 health centres reached.

The study gives no count or share of facilities entering their own reports nationally; it finds that yearly median completeness and timeliness of weekly, monthly and quarterly DHIS2 reports rose from 2016 to 2022 at national and South West Zone level but stayed below the 85% national target, Neno district passing it for monthly reports from 2019.

The study states that a DHIS2 system failure occurred in Malawi between March and August 2020, with a substantial drop in monthly report timeliness over those months, and cites a press report of the Ministry of Health losing management data.

The Ministry of Health's annual report shows the ministry running the HMIS on DHIS2 itself in 2023: it scaled up DHIS2 Mobile, trained clerks, supervised in every zone, ran in-office data quality assessments and had every district produce a bulletin from DHIS2, its digital health division working with CMED.

The Ministry of Health states that the expansion of DHIS2 Mobile to the 24 remaining districts in 2023 gave full coverage across the country, allowing direct data entry into DHIS2 by all health centres, and that DHIS2 aggregates performance data across all districts and health facilities.

The Ministry of Health states that the DHIS2 Mobile scale-up lets health centres enter data directly into DHIS2 where they previously sent it to district offices for entry, and records the outcome as real-time data entry at the facility level across all districts; it adds that many remote health centres have unreliable internet and some no power, which severely limits timely entry.

The Ministry of Health says the 2023 DHIS2 Mobile expansion allows direct entry by all health centres but gives no count or share of health centres entering their own reports; it gives staff trained (1,506 in one table, 1,560 clerks in another) and, for HMIS-15 reports in 2023, national completeness of 92.9% and timeliness of 73.5% (North Zone lowest at 87.8% and 53.1%).

The Ministry of Health reports that in 2023 DHIS2 Mobile was deployed in the 24 remaining districts, moving data entry from district offices to health centres, with 1,506 staff trained (939 data, ward or statistical clerks and 365 nurses, clinicians or facility in-charges) and an enhanced DHIS2 training for all data clerks and district coordinators after a system upgrade.

The Ministry of Health's annual report for fiscal year 2023-24 states that its digital health division is developing MaHIS, a comprehensive patient information system on OpenMRS design meant to manage all patients under one integrated system at all service delivery points; the fiscal year is the only date given.

The Ministry of Health states that the Health Sector Strategic Plan III (2023-2030), launched in January 2023, lists development of a shared electronic health record system among its reforms, and that this reform is being implemented through MaHIS.

The Ministry of Health states that MaHIS will scale up existing technology mostly supported by PEPFAR implementing partners and other donors; it names no domestic budget line for the system, saying only that budget lines for tablets and desktops are in donor and One Plan budgets; the fiscal year 2023-24 is the only date given.

The Ministry of Health states that the MaHIS emergency module, covering patient registration, triage and primary and secondary assessments, is being piloted at the QECH Adult Emergency and Trauma Centre; an outpatient module is developed and antenatal, NCD, immunisation and in-patient modules are under development, with no other site of use named; the fiscal year 2023-24 is the only date given.

The Ministry of Health names one MaHIS pilot site, the emergency centre of the QECH hospital, and states that the country has no reliable and functional outpatient system; it gives no count of primary clinics keeping an electronic patient record, only that 41% of health facilities use unnamed digital health technologies for service delivery; the fiscal year 2023-24 is the only date given.

The Ministry of Health reports as progress in fiscal year 2023-24 that the MaHIS emergency module was developed and put on pilot at QECH and the outpatient module developed, covering registration, vitals, consultation, diagnosis and prescription and integrated with dispensing and laboratory ordering.

The Global Fund's Inspector General states that the Fund has invested US$21 million in Malawi's Health Management Information System since Grant Cycle 4, yet the national system on DHIS2 is fully used only by the malaria and TB programmes, for three indicators, with about 90% of programmatic data still collected by hand on supervision visits budgeted at US$19.5 million in Grant Cycle 6; no domestic budget line is named. Dated to the audit, late 2023.

The Global Fund's Inspector General calls DHIS2 the national health management information system and names the Ministry of Health's Central Monitoring and Evaluation Division as the body that runs its data quality assessments, the last in 2021 with no evidence of follow-up; the audit covers January 2021 to June 2023.

The Global Fund's Inspector General states that since its 2019 audit mobile DHIS2 has been introduced in 15 districts, with over 2,000 tablets procured for the rollout and over 250 statistical clerks recruited and trained, and that timeliness and completeness of HIV, TB and malaria reporting have improved; it dates this only to the audit, on fieldwork of late 2023.

The Global Fund's Inspector General gives the mobile DHIS2 rollout as 15 districts and over 2,000 tablets, with no count or share of facilities entering their own reports; it found variances of 10% to 17% between DHIS2 and source registers for malaria data in the 16 facilities it visited, and notes that the malaria programme's DHIS2 data can be edited after the reporting period without review. Dated to the audit, late 2023.

The Global Fund's Inspector General states that about US$2.9 million allocated for data improvement in Grant Cycle 6 was moved to commodities because of delays in establishing an Electronic Medical Record policy, and that the country lacks a roadmap or strategy for integrating programme data systems; it names no general-care EMR system, the EMRs it names being the TB and HIV programmes' own.
